questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Australia is so far away from Denmark, so wanted to explore it and see all the stuff there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Would say it was easy enough.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Did not really require anything, but otherwise I could just have went by Stop1 at the campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The orientation is a little bit lacking, so you have to do most of the work yourself regarding getting friends and such. You are basically just invited to show up to get a water bottle and a grilled sausage on white toast..

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: The housing market is a total mess, so it is going to be really expensive to live there. Do not bother with Scape, live at the uni student accomodation if you want but it is also really expensive.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Housing market is extremely expensive and it is quite hard to find anything.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is expensive and no good opportunities.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Was quite easy, had to submit a study plan regarding which subjects I wanted to take and the academic requirements.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Don't know - did not need it.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Yes got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You can switch subjects in the first two weeks of the semester, so if you discover some subjects are bad, then you can switch them.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The master's degree programs at the Melbourne Business School are basically cash cows profiting from international students, so don't expect any Australians in your classes. And group assignments can be rather annoying due to the poor English skills of other students.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: 3 of my subjects were extremely easy and 1 of my subjects was quite hard.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style was generally quite bad compared to UCPH, with exams just being pure memorization and lectures just being lecturers reading from slides for 3 hours..

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Derivatives Securities
Applied Risk Management
Quantitative Analysis for Finance II
Macroeconometrics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Derivatives Securities: It was an extremely easy and boring version of Financial Decision Making; I can only recommend it if you want an easy subject during your exchange semester, as you do not need to study at all or follow the lectures to pass. You also need to buy a calculator.

Applied Risk Management: Was close to being the most boring subject I have ever had, as the lecturers just consisted of the lecturer reading the slides for 2-3 hours. The exam was basically doing Excel calculations by hand with a calculator, so you need to buy a calculator. I cannot really recommend it.

Quantitative Analysis for Finance II: The material itself should be quite interesting, but the lecturer was garbage, as he was using a previous lecturer's material and slides, but he did not understand anything about it, so any single time he was asked questions, he said it would get back to us, which he did not. It consists of three easy online tests on Canvas and then one final written research paper, so if you want to have one less exam, then go for it.

Macroeconometrics: is an extremely interesting and hard subject covering Bayesian econometrics in macroeconometrics and is basically a combination of a seminar in macro, the advanced macroeconometrics subject at UCPH, and a subject in Bayesian Econometrics. I required a constant high workload and would easily say that 95% of my studies at Melbourne were spent on this subject. The lecturer, Tomasz Wozniak, is quite entertaining and good, but he also demands quite a lot. I can recommend this subject if you want to challenge yourself during your exchange, but otherwise, do not consider this subject at all. It is quite hard and takes so much time.

questions.answer: Not sure if I encountered any unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Alcohol is so expensive, except from wine, so it is not that fun looking at your bank account day after a pub crawl.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are so many clubs at the uni, but because most of the domestic students are only takes the undergraduate degree; so almost all the clubs are just a bunch of undergraduate students.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Basically anything you can imagine, there was a whole week of clubs expo at campus, where you can meet all the clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Surfing club: they are so fun and hold a bunch of events 
Mountaneering club: You get a discount in outdoor shops if you join.
Social running club: Free coffee after a 3km run each friday.
Soccer club: Playing soccer with other international and some locals every saturday.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hiking in Victoria, travelling around in Australia. Go to Tasmania, Northern Queensland and go scuba diving at the Great Barrier Reef. Go to Sydney. Also head out to the outback and see Uluru, but there is no reason to be more 1 day at Uluru. Go surfing down in Torquay, head to Wilsons Prom. Great Ocean Road

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The student life is a bit weird as there is a clear divide between the domestic and international students, but the aussies are cool.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It can be a bit hard to socialize with the local students, because you can easily have classes, where there are no australians and you are the only non-asian student. There are also not any student bars at campus, so you kinda have to show up to club events and such to find australians, but they are easy enough to become friends with if you manage to find them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Australians are very friendly, but a lot of students at Uni Melb are not that social or outgoing, so can be a bit hard to get friends if you don't show up to everything.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The politeness and general niceness.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Live close to campus so you can attend events there. Travel a lot. Join clubs.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have a driver's license or prepare to find some friends, who will drive you around.  :)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting so many new friends and exploring and doing so much new stuff. Hiked so much on so many great trails. Took a Scuba diving certificate at the Great Barrier Reef, which was so worth it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being in a completely foreign country with no friends can be a bit hard when you just arrive.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
